rss.title: datasette 1.0a43
rss.summary: Release: datasette 1.0a43 I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone , which is now 53% complete. The biggest 1.0 item in this release is streaming support for output renderers - the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new Response.stream() method. There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory : private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed). There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation finally has a design suitable for 1.0 . A new <datasette-copy-button> Web Component provides copy-schema in various places. JSON in columns on the row page can be pretty-printed. There's a new DatasetteModal.confirm() JavaScript utility method. Plus dozens of bug fixes, including contributions by Zihan Dai , Peter Olkhovets , Ilya Khalafi , and Ankita Advitot . The feature I'm most excited about is a pretty tiny one: I've added CSS multi-page view transitions to Datasette! Here's the commit - key CSS is as follows: /* Enable cross-document view transitions, for anyone without prefers-reduced-motion */ @media ( prefers-reduced-motion : no-preference ) { @view-transition { navigation : auto ; } } /* .facet-results should morph from old position to new */ html : active-view-transition . content > . facet-results { view-transition-name : facet-results ; } /* So should a .table-wrapper, provided it contains .rows-and-columns */ html : active-view-transition . table-wrapper : has ( > table . rows-and-columns ) { view-transition-name : rows-table ; } With that in place, navigations within Datasette - still staunchly a multi-page application - feel more like an SPA. This works on Safari and Chrome at the moment and I believe supports for Firefox is due to land in Firefox 162 on December 8th 2026 (seeing as they are no longer feature-flagged in Firefox Nightly.) rss.summary: Release: datasette-llm 0.1a11 datasette-llm is the intermediate plugin for Datasette that supports configuring LLMs for use with other Datasette plugins. rss.title: Open-source AI without Jensen
rss.summary: A decapitation. It’s time to rebuild.
rss.text_excerpt:
The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a major setback for the US development of an open model ecosystem. Nvidia still has the financial interests in supporting open models, which are to avoid concentration in power among a few customers who would develop their own chips and reduce Nvidia’s profits, but supporting the open ecosystem is a tricky puzzle more than an engineering problem to grind out a solution on. Nvidia’s business operations are famously extremely dependent on Jensen as an operator, so it is a consensus opinion that there are challenges ahead (or even more high-profile departures through chip-smuggling investigations or plain-old sharks circling more poachable talent). Nvidia’s number one goal is to stabilize the ship, deliver to customers in the next 24 months, and prevent implosion. Open models have been one of Jensen’s more ambitious, founder-style bets. He has been flooding the zone with funding in a way that will very likely dry up. In this period, the open model economy is in its nascency. These are crucial years for establishing use-cases, revenue flow, and motives to continue training the next generation models. I discussed the sensitivity of these early years in my recent talk at Fireworks Forge ( slides , recording ). The core of the argument is one upside for open models, a reason to be optimistic, and one downside. The positive case is that the open model economy has correctly latched onto “ownership of intelligence” and enterprise post-training as a crucial lane. What is to be determined is exactly how big the downstream market is. The downside is that the true long-term benefit of open models, as truly commoditized intelligence, is very far from realization with compute in such short supply. In the near term, where inference startups are also struggling to get enough chips (because Anthropic and OpenAI are buying so much capacity), there’s little margin competition on open-weight models. If open-source models are also served at giant inference margins, as we learned with DeepSeek’s DeepInfer release, they’re far from a commodity. In this paradigm, the closed labs with better economies of scale and integration from model to datacenter and chips will win. I expanded on this challenge in my recent piece on the open model economy . Together, a lot still needs to go right for open models to be a meaningful economic engine. Jens

rss.title: datasette-leaflet 0.3
rss.summary: Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3 OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header . Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy. datasette-leaflet is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to strict-origin-when-cross-origin , passing the host but not the full path to the page. Tags: leaflet , datasette , openstreetmap

rss.title: AI Ambition: ArtCraft Cloned Photoshop and Now Wants to "Rebuild Everything"
rss.summary: ArtCraft used AI to rewrite Photoshop as open source software. For CEO Brandon Thomas, the vision is even bigger: to take back the internet!
rss.text_excerpt:
The theme of day two of the AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco was increasing ambition using AI . And there have been few projects as ambitious as ArtCraft in the AI era. So far the fledgling company has released 17 open source versions of popular software tools , starting with a Photoshop alternative built from scratch in Rust called PhotoCraft . You could feel the excitement in the room this morning when ArtCraft founder and CEO Brandon Thomas presented a kind of manifesto for AI-based open source at AIE Code. When he mentioned that ArtCraft had cloned Adobe’s Acrobat, with a product called PdfCraft, it got a round of applause from the audience. In wrapping up, his rallying cries of “let's take back the entire internet” and “let's rebuild everything” were greeted with whoops and cheers. Thomas began his presentation by reliving the internet’s early history. In his view, the web started out with the right intentions, but things got screwed up once Web 2.0 hit the mainstream. “We had a bunch of chat applications that were completely open,” he said, regarding the 1990s internet. “So, IRC is like Discord, but you can spin up your own servers that you actually own. You can use whatever programs to automate them and interrogate them without rules.” His point wasn’t necessarily that everything was open source, but that web users could freely build things. With Flash, for example — a commercial animation tool eventually acquired by Adobe — “kids were making all kinds of animations.” When Web 2.0 came along, with its superior broadband and smartphones, “it brought everybody into the fold.” Thomas acknowledged that this widened the scope of internet software, but at the cost of that freedom to build with leading apps. “The diffuse, experimental, early web started to disappear,” he said. “The APIs got taken away from us, and then we started seeing distribution being gatekept by the big providers.” It seems Adobe in particular annoyed Thomas. He described getting billed with an unexpected fee when he cancelled a monthly plan. “It's really frustrating that the web — that was once really, really promising and open and free — has turned into this extractive, owned, rent-seeking world.” This inspired him to start ArtCraft, “with the ethos of ‘let's build everything open source.’” A message even anti-AI people have gotten behind, according to Thomas. Octopus Superintelligence OS

A self-evolving agentic OS.
A new architecture for agent execution, built on operating-system principles, where agents can reshape their environment and the trajectory of their own work.

![Octopus OS](assets/octopus-os.gif) Octopus runs agents the way the well-known ones run: they read and write your files, drive a browser, use your desktop, call your apps and accounts. You talk to it by text or by voice. The difference is what they run on. You should never have to wonder whether it can do something. If it is allowed to, it can, and when it cannot yet, it can build itself the missing piece. Underneath, its architecture gives an agent a structure to execute in and a picture of itself and of the world. Capabilities are not add-ons bolted onto a loop. They are contracts in that architecture, so the system can grow in any direction - connect something new, give itself a new sense, rewrite itself. Neither the model nor the agent loop sits at the center. The kernel is about 45,000 lines of Rust; everything else is ported onto it, starting with Codex: sign in with ChatGPT and Codex CLI runs as one interface of the system. **Self-evolution** means shaping the conditions of future work. Under policy, an agent can create and revise goals, change interfaces (triggers), add tools, organize workers, and arrange context and execution environments. These changes persist across tasks and runs: they affect what it notices, when it acts, what it works on, and which capabilities it can use next. The agent changes its environment, and that environment shapes its subsequent behavior. **Self-improvement** remains the research aim: whether this process actually makes the system better. > [!NOTE] > This is a research preview. Agent orchestration, designed for Rex.
Threads and named agents, back in the terminal.

Install · Quick start · Docs · axel.md

--- ```sh # Two agents: one builds, one reviews with another model axel agent new terra codex axel agent new opus claude/opus # A thread: terra does the work, then hands the diff to opus axel thread new --agent terra "add retries to the webhook sender, then ask @opus for a review" ``` Or run `axel` in Rex and type the same thing into the launcher that floats over your window. The thread keeps going when you close the laptop, and you can pick it up from any machine. ## Key features ### 🧵 Threads, not chat tabs A thread is an intent and everything done about it. It outlives the agent's process, the pane and the machine: run several at once, resume tomorrow, settle it when it's done. Every change is a signed event, so copies on other machines merge. ### 🪪 Named agents A team of specialists instead of one assistant that knows everything. `terra` builds with a few skills for your stack; `opus` reviews with another model. Each has its own Ed25519 key, permissions, budget and inbox, and loads only its own skills. ```sh axel agent new opus claude/opus --skills review axel send "@opus please review the diff" ``` ### 🖥️ The terminal, fixed by Rex Agent apps rebuilt [TRUNCATED]
